Q: How to get email confirmation to work on Supabase local development environment A:

Had a similar issue where I wasn't receiving confirmation emails in my local environment. It turned out that the Auth service (GoTrue) didn't pick up the changes I made in my config.toml

I solved it by running supabase stop --no-backup and then supabase start, which forces the CLI to recreate the Docker containers and reload the configuration from scratch

Q: Google Sheets query function returning 0 when queried data returns empty and not treating it as ERROR A:

in this case you will need to use IFERROR because if your data has no entries between two selected dates the QUERY will throw you error not 0, therefore you do:


=IFERROR(QUERY(data; "select count(Col1) 
                      where Col5 >= date '"&TEXTO($A60; "yyyy-mm-dd")&"' 
                        and Col5 <= date '"&TEXTO(FIN.MES($A60; 0); "yyyy-mm-dd")&"' 
                      label count(Col1)''"; ); 0)

Q: Long-running 'py.test' stop at first failure A:

To programmatically fail immediately for specific tests only:

I used a variation of the "Incremental Testing" sample code from the docs: https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/example/simple.html#incremental-testing-test-steps

First, create a marker called 'critical'. I do this in pyproject.toml:

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
addopts = "-ra --strict-markers --strict-config"
markers = ['critical']  # Define custom markers here

Next, decorate any tests that should cause immediate termination on failure:

@pytest.mark.critical
def test_foo():
    assert False  # Put your actual test here

Now, in conftest.py, add the following:

critical_failure = ''  # Global name of critical test failure


def pytest_runtest_makereport(item, call):
    if 'critical' in item.keywords:  # Marker 'critical' was used
        if call.excinfo is not None:  # the test has failed
            global critical_failure  # Note global
            critical_failure = item.originalname or item.name  # Save test name


def pytest_runtest_setup(item):
    if critical_failure:  # If not empty, we now fail all remaining tests
        pytest.xfail(f"Critical test '{critical_failure}' failed")

Now when that specific test fails, you'll get an instant termination like:

=================tests/test_foo.py:31: AssertionError
=========== short test summary info ====================
XFAIL tests/test_file.py::test_bar - Critical test 'test_foo' failed
...
XFAIL tests/test_file.py::test_baz - Critical test 'test_foo' failed
FAILED tests/test_file.py::test_foo - assert False
============ 1 failed, 32 xfailed in 1.29s ==============

Which is quite nice.

If a failed test isn't marked with pytest.mark.critical pytest just continues running all other tests as usual.

Q: Swift extension example A:

2026 @ Swift 6.2.4

Using Custom Colors — No Extension Needed

Extensions are great for lots of things, but Suragch's original question was how to use custom colors in an app. Apple has made a lot of improvements in the past 10 years which make this much simpler to do.

Start by creating the custom colors in your apps Assets.xcassets file. Click the + button and select Color Set to create a new color. Give it whatever name you wish to for your custom color, with the first letter uppercase. When you use the color, you'll make the first letter lowercase.

Use the Inspector pane to choose whether you wish to include optional variants, or keep it simple with just Universal. From there, you have several ways to specify your exact color, including the good old Color Panel.

Now to use your custom colors, just use Color. and your custom color name with the first character lowercase. For example:

let foregroundColor = Color.praxButtonForeground

let backgroundColor = Color.praxButtonBackground

That's it!
